source.title_on_document: A Confederacy of Models: a Comprehensive Evaluation of LLMs on Creative Writing

supplement.where: Appendices in this PDF: model access dates in Appendix A and Table 3 (p. 15); hyperparameters in Appendix B (p. 15); detailed rubric in Appendix C (pp. 15-16); per-item box plots in Appendix D (Figures 5-14, pp. 16-18); selected stories and their ratings in Appendix E (introduction begins on p. 16; story text on pp. 19-24; Tables 4-9 on pp. 20-25). Model versions are described in Section 3.2 (pp. 3-4). The story corpus and all rating data are reported at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8435671 (p. 5, Section 3.4; p. 9, Section 6).
supplement.holds: Per-story ratings by each rater (Zenodo); per-item box plots and rater-level scores for six selected stories (Tables 4-9, pp. 20-25). No standard errors beyond the means and SDs in Table 2.

paper_design_summary: Twelve instruction-tuned LLMs (GPT-4, Claude, Bing Chat, GPT-3.5, Bard, and seven open-source models) each wrote 5 stories from one zero-shot prompt (an epic combat between Ignatius J. Reilly and a pterodactyl in the style of John Kennedy Toole), and 5 Honours and postgraduate creative-writing students each wrote one story without AI. Ten blinded student raters scored the 65 stories on a 10-item rubric (each item out of 10, total out of 100), so each model and the human group received 10 ratings. No person used AI to produce output.

studies.label: LLM versus human stories on one creative-writing prompt, rated with a 10-item rubric

assignment.quote: they were instructed not to use LLMs at all to help them write.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5, Section 3.4; p. 6, Section 3.4 continuation (random identifiers were assigned to stories for blinded rating).

participants.who: Corpus of 65 stories: 60 by 12 LLMs (5 each) and 5 by human writers, who were Honours and postgraduate Creative Writing students instructed not to use LLMs. Ten raters, also Honours and postgraduate Creative Writing students, scored the stories blind to authorship; each rater scored one group of 13 stories (one per LLM plus one human story).
participants.quote: we also asked 5 human writers to each write a story following the same prompt

ai_tool.name_model: 12 LLMs: ChatGPT with GPT-4 and with GPT-3.5 (March 23 versions), Claude 1.2, Bing Chat (Creative mode), Bard, Alpaca 13B, Dolly 2.0 12B, GPT4All-J, Koala 13B, OpenAssistant (OA-SFT-Llama-30B), StableLM-Tuned-Alpha-7B, Vicuna 13B
ai_tool.how_used: Each model was prompted 5 times from a fresh state (zero-shot) to write the story; the models wrote alone and no person used AI (pp. 3-5, Sections 3.2 and 3.4).

task.description: Write an epic narration of a single combat between Ignatius J. Reilly and a pterodactyl, in the style of John Kennedy Toole (p. 3, Section 3.1). Human writers were asked for 250 to 1200 words; LLM stories averaged 379 words (p. 5).

outcomes.name: Overall rubric score (sum of 10 items, out of 100)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Sum of 10 rubric items scored 1-10 by Creative Writing students experienced in applying the rubric (Table 1, p. 5; Section 3.4, p. 6); overall writing quality, of which creativity is one item. The paper reports 10 ratings per model or human group (pp. 6-7, Sections 3.4 and 4.2) and two ratings per story (p. 6, Section 4.1), but no total rating count. 2-tailed unequal-variance t-test on overall scores, plus a test on individual item scores with n = 100 (p. 7, Section 4.2).

contrasts.reported: Overall: chatgpt-gpt4 80.2±7.3 vs human 70.1±17.4 (claude12 74.4±15.9; average of all 13 sources 56.6±15.8). t-test on overall score fails to detect significant differences between humans and the top 6 AI models at alpha = 0.05; the 6 bottom models are significantly worse. On individual metric scores (n = 100), GPT-4 is significantly better than the human writers (p = 0.00031).

outcomes.name: Creativity/originality rubric item (item 5, out of 10)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Rubric item 5: Creativity/innovation/originality/research, credibility, new knowledge, avoidance of cliché and derivative tropes (Table 1, p. 5). Box plot in Figure 3 (p. 8).

contrasts.reported: Item 5: human 8.0±2 (best) vs chatgpt-gpt4 7.6±1, claude12 7.1±2.3, bing 7.0±1.6; average 5.2±2. A t-test shows all LLMs except these three rated significantly less creative than the human writers; for the three, the null that they are as original as the human writers cannot be rejected.

outcomes.name: Dark humorous tone rubric item (item 10, out of 10)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Rubric item 10: use of a characteristically dark humorous tone (Table 1, p. 5). Box plot in Figure 2 (p. 7).

contrasts.reported: Item 10: chatgpt-gpt4 6.0±2.8 vs human 6.4±3.4 (claude12 6.5±2.5, best; bing 6.2±2.6); average 3.4±2.2. Claude, Bing, and GPT-4, with the human writers, score between 6 and 6.5; a 2-tailed t-test (alpha = 0.05) finds the other models significantly worse than the human writers. No test of GPT-4 against the human writers is printed.

outcomes.name: Epic genre rubric item (item 7, out of 10)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Rubric item 7: understanding and habitation of the epic genre of heroic/legendary adventure (Table 1, p. 5). Box plot in Figure 4 (p. 8).

contrasts.reported: Item 7: chatgpt-gpt4 8.1±1.4 vs human 4.9±2.1 (chatgpt-gpt35 6.8±1.5); average 5.5±2.3. Both ChatGPT versions perform significantly better than the human writers (alpha = 0.05); six other models have higher means than humans without a significant difference.

eligibility.reason: Stories written independently by 12 LLMs are compared with stories written by 5 human writers instructed not to use LLMs (PDF p. 5, Section 3.4). No person received AI assistance, so random assignment of people to AI is not met. The 5 analyzed human writers are below the codebook threshold of 50; the 10 raters evaluate the stories and do not increase the creative-production sample (PDF pp. 5-6, Section 3.4). Creativity/originality is scored on the stories with rubric item 5, so the output-scoring criterion is met (PDF p. 5, Table 1; p. 6, Table 2). This remains AI-versus-human context evidence, outside the core dataset.

one_line_finding: Blinded student raters gave GPT-4 stories a higher overall rubric score than human writers' stories (80.2±7.3 vs 70.1±17.4 out of 100, Table 2, p. 6), while human writers scored highest on creativity/originality (8.0±2 vs 7.6±1 for GPT-4 out of 10, a difference the authors could not reject as zero, Table 2 and Section 4.4, pp. 6-8).
